transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2028-01-12
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~67 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen, Diego Alvarez, Evelyn Park (Redwood); Tom Reynolds, Aisha Patel, Liam O'Connor, Sara Ng (NimbleCare)
---
Summary (auto): Focus on private VPC networking interactions with Redwood Private runtime. Walked through resolver ordering, privatelink route tables, NAT hairpin, and KV cache/batching impact. Collected highest risk items: split-horizon resolver misconfig, missing route for privatelink interface, and SNAT timeouts.
---
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros, then Diego will take us through the path-trace examples.
[00:10] Tom (NimbleCare): Hi, Tom here — infra. We saw intermittent 500s from the redwood runtime, mostly during heavy batch bursts.
[00:20] Diego (Redwood): Got it. Quick question, do you run Redwood Private inside EKS or on EC2 flat instances?
[00:27] Tom: EKS. Fargate for some batch workers, but the inference pods are on EC2 nodes in a private subnet.
[00:34] Maya: And you said these 500s correlate with outbound calls — is that to S3, KMS, or to Redwood control plane or both?
[00:43] Sara (NimbleCare): Mostly control plane endpoints, the VPC endpoint we set up for redwood API is via Privatelink but we still see egress to public internet for telemetry to our logging endpoint — which is odd.
[00:56] Diego: Okay that's a key signal. We're going to show a couple of misconfig patterns: split-horizon DNS where the resolver returns private endpoint sometimes and public IP other times; and hairpin NAT where pod talks to privatelink but reply path leaves via NAT.
[01:10] Liam (Security): Quick add — we have strict egress policy and a proxy that rewrites some ipv6 to ipv4 which might be causing flapping.
[01:19] Diego: Alright, I'll start with a simple diagram. (small pause) So imagine pod > node kernel > route table. If Privatelink is in a different AZ and route target is the ENI, the route table must include the prefix for the endpoint, otherwise traffic goes to NAT gateway. That creates asymmetric routing.
[01:40] Tom: We do have a shared NAT per AZ and a central privatelink in a different account. Is that a red flag?
[01:47] Diego: Not inherently, but it increases chance of asymmetric return path. If the packet leaves the pod and hits the privatelink ENI in AZ-a, but reply is SNATed through NAT in AZ-b, TCP state mismatches show up as timeouts and 5xx.
[02:05] Maya: Also DNS — if the resolver sometimes resolves the privatelink host to a public ip, requests may bypass the endpoint entirely.
[02:12] Aisha (Platform): Our CoreDNS has forwarders to two resolvers: the VPC resolver and a corporate resolver. Could that produce mixed answers?
[02:21] Diego: Yes — that's split-horizon in practice. If you have conditional forwarding and one resolver has a stale record, your client may flip between targets. On top of that, our runtime relies on consistent KV cache hits. If the first request goes to public, the KV miss adds latency, then subsequent requests may hit private endpoint and see different session affinity.
[02:45] Sara: That sounds like the sort of churn we saw. We also observed that when batch sizes grow above 8, latency spikes dramatically.
[02:52] Diego: One path is that larger batches keep KV cache open longer but require more egress throughput for model shards, so if egress RTT increases you see token generation stalls.
[03:04] Tom: Can you walk us through a traceroute example? We ran one but it was noisy and the team wasn't sure how to interpret it.
[03:11] Diego: Yeah I'll narrate a sample. I'll paste a canonical trace later but here: [03:15] pod -> node -> ENI -> privatelink-eni (local) -> redwood endpoint. If route table misses the privatelink prefix it goes pod -> node -> natgw -> internet -> redwood pub ip, and return path -> privatelink eni, creating asymmetry. You may see that hop counts look odd and some hops show firewall drop.
[03:36] Tom: We do have firewall rules that block 10.x/16 between AZs for some tenants. That could be the drop.
[03:43] Diego: That explains it. Also check MTU mismatches — if privatelink encapsulates, reduction in MTU can cause fragmenting and slowdown for large batched payloads.
[03:55] Aisha: Oof, we definitely have a 1500 MTU on some virtual interfaces and jumbo on others.
[04:01] Diego: Okay thing to check: ICMP 'fragmentation needed' isn't always visible to apps. Run path MTU discovery or increase logs.
[04:10] Maya: Let's pivot to DNS ordering. Diego, can you explain how resolver order interacts with the runtime's hostname caching?
[04:17] Diego: Sure. Redwood Private runtime uses short-lived connect pooling and relies on local glibc resolver caches plus the app-level host cache. If glibc resolves IP-A first and caches it for N seconds, then the app reuses it. If resolver flips during that time, new connections may go elsewhere but existing pooled connections remain. So you can get a mixture of routes within the same minute. That's rough for consistent session affinity with KV cache.
[04:44] Sara: Is there a recommended TTL or cache-control to set server side?
[04:49] Diego: We recommend consistent internal DNS with low TTLs only if you have consistent routing. For private endpoints, prefer returning private IPs and pinning route tables so the answer always maps to reachable ENIs.
[05:00] Liam: From a security standpoint, could we favour SNI and mTLS so if it goes public we still authenticate?
[05:07] Maya: Absolutely. mTLS is a good fallback, but it doesn't solve asymmetry and SNAT state issues. It just protects the channel.
[05:14] Tom: We also saw some 503s when pods communicate with other local services behind an internal ALB. Any connection to that relate?
[05:22] Diego: Yes — internal ALBs rely on source IP sometimes for routing decisions; SNAT changes source and can break sticky sessions. Also, if your nodes use different NATs depending on AZ, affinity breaks.
[05:33] Aisha: We have sticky sessions on some telemetry endpoints. Should we remove stickiness?
[05:37] Diego: Either remove or ensure source IPs are preserved via e.g., proxy targets in the same AZ or use ENI routing.
[05:44] Maya: Let's pause — I'm hearing three immediate items: DNS split-horizon, asymmetric routing due to route table/NAT configuration, and MTU/fragmentation. Is that fair?
[05:53] Tom: Yep.
[05:55] Diego: Now, practical debugging. We recommend: 1) run curl from pod and node and compare destination IP, 2) run traceroute from both, 3) capture tcpdump on node ENI and natgw. Also, collect control plane logs from Redwood runtime — connection opens, TLS SNI, and upstream IP.
[06:12] Tom: We'll do that. One detailed question: how does KV cache behavior change when DNS resolution flips mid-traffic?
[06:18] Diego: Great question. KV cache keys are usually based on model+prefix+session. If requests land on two different backend IPs, KV cache replication isn't instant. Two cases: if backends are independent, you'll get misses and duplicated work. If there's a shared KV store behind the endpoint then consistency is fine. But we've seen customer infra where the privatelink endpoint hits different backends with local cache and no shared replication, causing token-level regressions.
[06:43] Sara: That could explain hallucination-like behavior during spikes — model restarts or misses.
[06:47] Diego: Exactly. Also batching: the runtime tries to batch requests within a small window (10-50ms). If egress RTT is high, that window can overrun and the batch scheduler changes behavior — either flushes early or creates giant coalesced batches that increase tail latency.
[07:04] Aisha: Are there knobs we can tune in Redwood runtime to be resilient?
[07:08] Diego: Yes — you can reduce max batch size, tighten batch delay, enable per-route circuit breaker, and prefer connection reuse. We can propose a profile: max_batch 8, batch_delay_ms 25, aggressive connection pooling, and keep-alive tuned to 60s for your environment.
[07:27] Tom: Regarding quantization — we saw CPU fallback during spikes. Is that related?
[07:32] Diego: Possibly. Quantized kernels are sometimes more sensitive to memory bandwidth. If the underlying node faces high network-induced IO wait (e.g., page-ins, sharded model download), CPU fallback can occur. On top of that, if the runtime tries to fetch weights from S3 via a slow NAT path, load stalls. So ensure model caches are pinned locally and pre-warmed.
[07:55] Liam: For pre-warming, any safe pattern for our security posture? We can't have S3 public reads.
[08:01] Diego: Use VPC endpoint for S3 with proper policy, or replicate artifacts into private S3 in the same account with restrictive ACLs. The key is low-latency access to model weights — avoid cross-account public pulls at runtime.
[08:14] Maya: Back to DNS — Aisha, can you share your CoreDNS config after the call? We want to look for conditional_forward and stubDomains.
[08:21] Aisha: Sure I'll send it.
[08:23] Diego: One debugging trick: run 'dig +trace' and compare resolver answers across nodes in each AZ. Also use 'getent hosts' to see nscd/glibc caching.
[08:33] Tom: We'll collect that.
[08:35] Evelyn (Redwood CS): We'll also attach our runbook for NAT hairpin checks — it has the tcpdump filters and command list.
[08:42] Tom: Great.
[08:44] Diego: Now a short demo of an observable we recommend to surface these problems quickly: instrument open connections in runtime metrics — upstream_ip, upstream_rtt_ms, batch_size, kv_hit_rate. If you see upstream_ip flipping and kv_hit_rate dropping during the same window, that's the clue.
[09:03] Sara: Do you have a Grafana or example query?
[09:06] Diego: Yes — we'll send example PromQL: rate(upstream_connection_open_total[1m]) by (upstream_ip), plus histogram of upstream_rtt_ms and kv_hit_rate.
[09:18] Maya: Quick security note — if you plan to run packet captures we'll have a template to redact PII and keys. Liam?
[09:25] Liam: We'll follow that.
[09:27] Tom: Any immediate config changes you recommend as a stop-gap?
[09:31] Diego: If you can, prefer colocating Privatelink endpoints in each AZ and update route tables to point to endpoint network interface per-AZ. If not immediately possible, pin certain critical hosts to use the corporate proxy that preserves source IP. Also lower max_batch from 16 to 8 for now.
[09:48] Aisha: We'll lower batch sizes tonight.
[09:50] Diego: Great. Also run a small KV-cache microbench where you simulate 200 concurrent requests with two different upstream IPs and measure kv_hit_rate under 5-second runs — that'll surface cache replication issues.
[10:05] Tom: On the traceroute artifacts — we have some traces showing a 200ms hop when traffic crosses AZs. Is that acceptable?
[10:12] Diego: 200ms is high for intra-region AZ hops; looks like traffic going over internet or transitive peering. Ideally intra-AZ should be <5ms, intra-region <20ms. 200ms explains token stalls and batch flushes.
[10:26] Sara: One last item — DNS TTL. Some of our records use 60s TTLs but the corporate resolver overrides to 5s. Could that cause flip?
[10:34] Diego: Yes, if corporate resolver returns different answers, short TTL means frequent flips which increases mixer of backends. For runtime heavy traffic prefer stable mapping.
[10:43] Maya: Let's recap quick. Action items and next steps were captured — Maya to send diagram/runbook; Diego to prepare KV lab; NimbleCare to collect traceroutes, tcpdumps, and CoreDNS config. We'll schedule a follow-up in one week to review artifacts.
[10:58] Tom: Thanks all. Anything else?
[11:01] Liam: If you can include example IAM policy for S3 privatelink access that'd be helpful.
[11:07] Maya: We'll attach sample policy. Thanks everyone.
[11:10] (call ends)
